intro.heading: The form was filled in. Does anyone know what it says?
intro.sub: A scenario we see in many care settings.
intro.paragraph: Margaret moves into a care home on a Monday. Her daughter brings a photo of the garden she kept for forty years and a long list of small things: tea strong, radio on low, never a bath before breakfast. The manager promises to write it all up. By Thursday a this is me form exists, but it sits in a folder in the office. The night carer has never seen it. On Friday Margaret is distressed at bedtime and nobody knows that humming her favourite hymn settles her. Here is how it plays out.

trail.text: Margaret moves in. Her daughter brings photos and a long list.
The manager listens properly and promises to write it all down.
A this is me form is filled in and put in her file.
The night carer has never seen it and has no time to go and look.
Her son remembers the hymn that calms her. Nobody has asked him.
Margaret is upset. The carer tries things that do not help.
The form is in a folder. New staff have never heard of it.
“How do you know what matters to each person?” A folder is not an answer.

trail_close: The form was never the problem. The gap is between the page and the person on shift at night. Here is how CareStream closes it, and where it stops.

why.heading: A form in a file does not help the carer at the bedside
why.sub: The detail only matters if the right person has it at the right moment.

cards.title: Families know things you cannot guess
cards.body: The hymn, the favourite chair and the name she likes to be called live in the family's heads. Without a simple way to ask, they stay there.

cards.title: Paper is out of reach at 3am
cards.body: Night staff, agency staff and new starters rarely open a folder. They need the answer in the moment, in words they can read quickly.

cards.title: Profiles go stale
cards.body: People change. A page written in week one is wrong by month six unless someone adds to it, and nothing nudges anyone to do so.

talk.heading: The questions managers ask, and how CareStream answers them
talk.sub: Read this as a conversation. The questions are the ones we hear most.

items.q: We already do a this is me form on paper. Why change?
items.a: Paper is fine for the first conversation. The trouble comes later, when night staff and new starters never see it and nobody updates it. CareStream keeps the same kind of detail where staff can ask about it in seconds, and where you can keep adding.

items.q: Is this the same as the printed this is me form?
items.a: No. CareStream has its own resident profile with 11 sections. It does not replace any form you already use, and we do not claim it is that form.

Life story, interests, likes and dislikes, food and drink they enjoy, daily routine, what helps when they are upset, how they like to communicate, important people and pets, faith and culture, and anything else. It is about who the person is, not their clinical record.
Yes. You invite them by name and email and they get a private link, valid for 14 days. They answer a question for each section. You check every answer before the care team can see it.

items.q: What can a carer actually do with it?
items.a: In the Staff Hub they pick the This is me topic and ask about a resident by name. The answer comes from the approved profile only. If the detail is not there, the hub says so rather than guessing.
No. For anything clinical, such as medication, diet texture or mobility, it points back to the care plan and the nurse or senior on shift. The profile is about the person, not their treatment.

limits.heading: A way to know the person, not a care record

cards.title: It is not your care plan
cards.body: The profile holds who someone is. Risks, medication and clinical needs stay in your care plan, and the hub assistant sends clinical questions back there.

cards.title: Families do not get a login
cards.body: They answer through a private link that lasts 14 days. They cannot see the profile or message staff, and a new link is needed to add more.

cards.title: It only knows what you put in
cards.body: If a detail is not in the approved profile, the hub says it is not recorded yet. Someone still has to ask, listen and write it down.

faqs.heading: This is me and resident profiles, answered

items.q: What should go in a this is me document?
items.a: The things that tell a carer who the person is: their history, routines, likes, what calms them, who matters and what they believe in. Our guide, the this is me document explained, goes through it in detail.

items.q: Is a this is me form the same as a resident profile?
items.a: They do the same job, which is helping staff know the person. A this is me form is usually a printed document. CareStream's version is an online record with 11 sections that staff can ask about.

items.q: What is life story work in a care home?
items.a: It is the practice of learning and recording a person's history, so care fits who they are. A short, true profile is a good start. It does not need to be long to be useful.
Admins manage it. Staff can see living residents who have at least one section filled in, through the hub. Unapproved family answers are never shown to staff.

items.q: How many residents can I add?
items.a: Up to 500 living residents. Each section holds up to 6,000 characters.

items.q: Does staff training on dementia still matter?
items.a: Yes. A profile tells staff about one person. Training builds the skills to support anyone. See the dementia awareness course.

items.q: Will an inspector expect to see this?
items.a: Care must reflect people's preferences. Regulation 9 says care and treatment must be appropriate, meet needs and reflect preferences. A profile is one way to show you know them. It is not a pass and it is not a regulator record.

items.q: What does CQC say about preferences and cultural needs?
items.a: The CQC guidance on Regulation 9 expects care to be based on an assessment of needs and preferences, including cultural, religious and spiritual needs. Your profile can hold that detail, and your care plan stays the formal record.

guide.heading: A practical way to build a profile with a family
guide.lede: The best profiles are short, true and kept up to date. You do not need to capture a whole life in a week. Start with what helps staff do the next shift well.

sections.h3: Life story work that fits a busy week
paragraphs: Life story work can feel like a big project, so many homes put it off. Start small. Ask three questions in the first week: what do you like to be called, what does a good day look like, and what calms them when they are upset. Add the longer history over time, with the family, as you get to know the person.
Ask the person first, where they can tell you. Family memories add colour, but the resident's own voice comes first.

sections.h3: Four checks for the first fortnight
checklist: Day one: add the person with the name they like to be called, and fill in what helps when they are upset.
Within a week: invite one or two family members or friends to answer the questions.
Each answer: read it, edit if needed and approve it before staff see it.
Each month: add one new detail you have learned, so the profile keeps pace with the person.

guide.note: For the inspector. Keep the profile separate from the care plan. The profile shows what matters to the person, and the care plan shows how you meet their needs.
